newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British Business - Dec 23.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British Business - Dec 23.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company

-- SAINTS GIVE FROST OFFER CHILLY RESPONSE Southampton Football Club have rejected an attempt by Sir David Frost to buy a stake in the club. A consortium headed by the broadcaster made the approach via merchant bank UBS, and offered to finance a new ground. The club rejected the offer as over 50 per cent of the club's shareholders have already agreed to a reverse takeover by Secure Retirement.

-- WHITE KNIGHT 'UNLIKELY' FOR CLYDE PETROLEUM A white knight is unlikely to save Clyde Petroleum from the bid by Gulf Canada Resources, the Gulf chief executive said in the weekend. However, Clyde's price climbed to 119.5p on Friday, well ahead of Gulf's 105p cash offer.

-- USAIR SHARE BUYBACK HITS LEGAL TURBULENCE Legal doubts were cast in the weekend on the chances of the 23 per cent stake British Airways is trying to sell in USAir being bought by the American company itself. USAir is incorporated in Delaware and the company is unlikely to meet the financial standards required by the state.

-- FEES SMASH 1 BILLION POUND BARRIER Fees earned by City players from takeover and merger action will top 1 billion pounds stg this year, compared to 950 million pounds last year. The situation is likely to continue as takeovers from the late rush of bids occur in early 1997.

-- NORTHERN POISED TO APPEAL OVER EXTENSION OF CE BID Northern Electric will this morning make a last attempt to ward off the takeover bid from CE Electric with a bid to the Takeover Panel. After the Panel extended the bid deadline from Friday to midday Monday, CE was able to acquire the 50 per cent minimum of Northern shares.

-- NATWEST SUSPENDS 18 STAFF NatWest has suspended 18 of its insurance operation staff over allegations they had sold themselves backdated Norwich Union shares in an attempt to cash in on the upcoming Norwich flotation. The allegations emerged after an internal investigation.

-- FAMILIES MISS OUT ON WORK The Labour Party last night said the growing number of jobless single parents means that three million children will spend Christmas without a job earner in the house. The announcement was made in an attempt to take the shine off the government's attempt to capitalize on falling unemployment figures.

-- FUND MANAGERS SEEK END TO FAT-CAT DEALS The National Association of Pension Funds will today say that all directors should be required to put themselves up for regular re-election, and that shares with less than full voting rights should be phased out. The organization is urging the Hampel Committee on corporate governance to limit golden handshakes by restricting directors' contracts to one year.

-- ROVER PLANS LINK-UP WITH CHRYSLER A link-up between Rover and Chrysler may be announced in the not-too-distant future. Talks between the two companies as well as BMW, Rover's parent, have been going on for some weeks. BMW and Chrysler have already combined on a deal to supply Mini engines from a plant in Brazil.

-- PEARSON REFUSES TO EXPAND INTO FOOTBALL Pearson has rejected an approach by the head of its television subsidiary, Greg Dyke, to consider buying into a top football club. The rejection is thought to be the last act of the current directors under Lord Blakenham. The future status of Pearson TV is undergoing a review as the company prepares for Marjorie Scardino to become chief executive in a fortnight.

-- LILLEY URGED TO KEEP GAS PAYMENT SCHEME The Gas Consumers Council and independent gas suppliers have urged Social Security Secretary Peter Lilley not to discontinue a scheme which helps poorer families pay their heating bills. They say such a move will disrupt competition by encouraging companies to 'cherry-pick' more affluent customers.

-- ITALY MOVES CLOSER TO JOINING EMU Italy's attempt to be among the countries to join the first wave of European monetary union yesterday moved closer when its parliament passed an austerity budget designed to meet EMU criteria. The budget will cut 62,500bn lire from next year's budget with a regional levy for companies and an unpopular new 'Euro tax.'
